¶
'''welt-trimmer''' (welt′trim″ėr), ''n.'' A cutting-tool for trimming welts for shoes; also, a welt-machine.

'''wel-willy†''', ''a.'' See ''well-willy''.

'''Welwitschia''' (wel-wich′i-ä), ''n.'' [NL. (J. D. Hooker, 1863), named after Friedrich ''Welwitsch'' (1806–72), an Austrian botanist and traveler.] A genus of gymnospermous plants, of the order ''Gnetaceæ'', among the most remarkable in the vegetable kingdom, distinguished by diœcious many-flowered imbricated cone-like spikes panicled at the margin of a short woody trunk. {{smaller|The only species, ''W. mirabilis'', is a native of sandy regions of southwestern tropical Africa, in Benguela and Damara-land, between 14° and 23° south latitude.}}

'''wem<sup>1</sup>†''' (wem), ''v. t.'' [< ME. ''wemmen'', < AS. ''wemman'' (= OHG. ''gi-wemman'' = Goth. ''ana-wammjan''), spot, blemish, etc., < ''wam'' (''wamm-''), a spot: see ''wem''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.''] To corrupt; vitiate. ''Drant.''

'''wem<sup>2</sup>†''' (wem), ''n.'' [A shortened form of ''weam'', ''wame'', a dial. form of ''womb''.] The belly; the wame.
{{smaller block|<poem>He bad his gang therefore command us . . .
To probe its [the Trojan horse’s] ''wem'' with wedge and beetle.</poem>
{{right|''Cotton'', Scarronides, p. 7. (''Davies''.)}}}}

'''wemless†''' (wem′les), ''a.'' [< ME. ''wemles'', ''wemmeles'', ''wemlees'', < AS. ''wamleás'', ''womleás'', without spot or blemish, < ''wam'', spot, + ''-leás'' = E. ''-less''.] Spotless; stainless; immaculate.
{{smaller block|<poem>Thou Virgin ''wemmeles'',
Bar of thy body, and dweltest mayden pure.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Second Nun’s Tale, l. 47.}}}}

'''wemmy†''' (wem′i), ''a.'' [< ''wem''<sup>1</sup> + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Faulty; unsound; blemished; tainted.
{{smaller block|The mustie wheate, the sowre wine, the ratt-eaten bread, the ''wemmie'' cheese.
{{right|''Guevara'', Letters (tr. by Hellowes, 1577), p. 257.}}}}

'''wen''' (wen), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wen'', ''wenne'', < AS. ''wen'', ''wæn'' (''wenn-'', ''wænn-'') = OFries. ''wen'' = D. ''wen'' = LG. ''wen'', ''ween'' = G. dial. ''wenne'', ''wehne'', ''wähne'', a wen, wart.] A circumscribed benign tumor of moderate size, occurring on any part of the body, but especially on the scalp, consisting of a well-defined sac inclosing sebaceous matter.

'''wenny''' (wen′i), ''a.'' [< ''wen'' + ''-y''<sup>1</sup>.] Same as ''wennish''. ''Wiseman'', Surgery.

'''wenona''' (wē-nō′nä̤), ''n.'' [N. Amer. Ind.] A small American serpent, ''Charina plumbea'', native of California and Mexico. {{smaller|It is a sort of sand-snake related to and formerly placed in the family ''Erycidæ'', but represents a different family, ''Charinidæ''.}}

'''went<sup>1</sup>†''' (went), ''n.'' [< ME. ''wente''; < ''wend''<sup>1</sup> (cf. ''bent''<sup>1</sup>, ''n.'', < ''bend''<sup>1</sup>).] '''1.''' A turn or change of course; a turning or veering; hence, a rolling or tossing about.
{{smaller block|<poem>In wo to bedde he wente,
And made or it was day ful many a ''wente''.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Troilus, ii. 63.}}
<poem>He knew the diverse ''went'' of mortall wayes.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., VI. vi. 3.}}}}
'''2.''' A course; a passage; a path.
{{smaller block|<poem>Hit forth wente
Doun by a floury grene ''wente''
Ful thikke of gras, ful softe and sweet.</poem>
{{right|''Chaucer'', Death of Blanche, l. 398.}}
<poem>But here my wearie teeme, nigh over spent,
Shall breath it selfe awhile after so long a ''went''.</poem>
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., IV. v. 46.}}}}
'''3.''' A furlong of land. ''Halliwell.''

See ''well-willy''. '''Welwitschia''' (wel-wich′i-ä), ''n.''   [NL. (J. D. Hooker, 1863), named after Friedrich ''Welwitsch'' (1806–72), an Austrian botanist and traveler.]   A genus of gymnospermous plants, of the order ''Gnetaceæ'', among the most remarkable in the vegetable kingdom, distinguished by diœcious many-flowered imbricated cone-like spikes panicled at the margin of a short woody trunk. {{smaller|The only species, ''W. mirabilis'', is a native of sandy regions of southwestern tropical Africa, in Benguela and Damara-land, between 14° and 23° south latitude.}} Its thick trunk bears but two leaves. The original coty{{smaller|ledons, which are opposite, green, spreading, and persistent, are composed of a hard fibrous substance, and become often 6 feet long and 2 or 3 wide. They finally split into long shreds, but are still retained, it is said, through over a hundred years of growth. The mature trunk forms a tabular mass only about a foot high, but 5 or 6 feet across; the top is truncate, hard, pitted, and broken by cracks, and resembles a fungus of the genus ''Polyporus;'' the base is deeply sunk in the soil, and produces middle-sized roots. The panicled inflorescence is composed of rigid erect dichotomously jointed stems from 6 to 12 inches high, with two opposite scales sheathing each joint, and is developed annually from the upper side of the trunk at the base of the cotyledons. The flower-spikes are composed of brilliant scarlet scales overlapping, usually in four rows — the male with spikes 1½ inches long or under, the female larger, fewer, and thicker. Each scale contains a flower, the male a small loose membranous perianth, the filaments connate into a loosely exserted tube, and six anthers, each opening by three apical and finally confluent pores. The fruit is dry, two-winged, compressed, inclosed in a fibrous utricle. The new growth is chiefly horizontal, enlarging the stem both above and below the base of the leaf, which finally projects from a deep marginal cavity.}} [[File:century v08 p0683 c1f1.png|center|316px]] {{c|{{smaller|''Welwitschia mirabilis.''
